d: The scope of a variable or function is the block of code that can access it.
h:
In scripting, a block of code is the body of a control structure or function. The scope of a variable or function is the block of code that can access it, and it can be global or local. All blocks can access global variables and functions. A block can access local variables and functions in its parent block, but not in any of its child blocks.

Variables and functions have global scope by default, but it's almost always better to declare them with local scope because Luau accesses local variables and functions faster than global ones. To give a variable or function local scope, put the keyword local before its name when you declare it.

Scripts cannot access global and local variables or functions in other scripts. If you want to share values and functions between scripts, use ModuleScripts.

local helloWorld = 'Hello World!'
local function printHelloWorld()
    print(helloWorld)
end
printHelloWorld() -- Hello World!

  • Block B can access the local variable in block A.
  • Block C can access the local variables and functions in blocks A and B.
  • Block A cannot access the local variables and functions in blocks B or C.
  • Block B cannot access the local variable in block C.

Global scope

After you declare a global variable or function, any block of code in the same script can access it. Variables and functions have global scope unless you declare them with the local keyword.

In the following code, testVar has global scope within the local testFunc() function. When Luau calls the testFunc(), it assigns testVar the value 64. The testVar has global scope, so the print() function outside testFunc() can access it and print 64.

local function testFunc()  -- local scope
    testVar = 64  -- global scope
end

testFunc()

print(testVar) -- 64

In the following code, the global variable x starts at 0, increments by 1 with each iteration of the for loop, and prints again afterward with a final value of 4.

x = 0  -- Global variable "x"

for i = 1, 4 do
    x += 1
    print("Global 'x' = " .. x)
end

print("Global 'x' = " .. x)

--[[ Resulting output:
Global 'x' = 1
Global 'x' = 2
Global 'x' = 3
Global 'x' = 4
Global 'x' = 4
]]

It's easier to declare global variables and functions because you don't need to type as much, but global variables and functions have the following disadvantages compared to local ones:

  • Luau accesses global variables and functions with a hash lookup, so it's expensive to use in terms of performance. Using a global variable in a time-critical loop can make it perform more than 10% slower than using a local variable in the same loop.
  • Luau disposes of local variables after their scope ends, reducing memory usage.
  • You can access global variables and functions within the same script, but not between multiple scripts. Therefore, a global variable or function doesn't provide any benefit over an in-scope local equivalent, an upvalue, or a shadow.

Local scope

Luau can only access a local variable or function in the block of code where you declare it. Creating a variable with local scope gives you tighter control over when and where its value changes.

In the following code, the testFunc() function and testVar variable have local scope. Only the code within testFunc() can access the testVar variable. The testVar variable doesn't have a value outside testFunc(), so calling print(testVar) within testFunc() prints the value of testVar, but calling print(testVar) outside testFunc() prints nil.

local function testFunc()  -- local scope
    local testVar = 64  -- local scope
    print(testVar) -- 64
end

testFunc()

print(testVar) -- nil

In the following code, the local variable x has value 0 at line 1. As Luau iterates through the for loop, a different local variable x has value 1. Then, Luau prints the initial variable x with an unchanged value 0.

local x = 0  -- Local variable "x"

for i = 1, 4 do
    local x = 1  -- Different variable "x", local to this "for" loop
    print("Loop 'x' = " .. x)
end

print("Initial 'x' = " .. x)

--[[ Resulting output:
Loop 'x' = 1
Loop 'x' = 1
Loop 'x' = 1
Loop 'x' = 1
Initial 'x' = 0
]]

const variables and functions follow the same scope rules as local ones. You can declare them in any block, including inside another function. For more information on const, see Const variables.

Capture

After you declare and assign a local variable, you can read it in its scope level and functions whose scopes is enclosed by the same scope containing the local variable. This technique is known as capturing.

In the following code, the function f captures the local variable x. The variable x in f() is an upvalue.

local x = 5

local function f()
    print(x)
end

f() -- 5
print(x) -- 5

Shadow

After you declare and assign a local variable, you can read it in its scope level and descendant scope levels. If you redeclare and reassign the variable in a descendant scope level, then you create a new local variable with the same name but different value from the most previous assignment. The new local variable doesn't affect the local variable from the previous assignment. This technique, known as shadowing, helps you reuse the name of a variable without reusing its value.

In the following code, Luau shadows the variable x. The variable x in f() is a shadow variable.

local x = 5

local function f()
    local x = 7
    print(x)
end

f() -- 7
print(x) -- 5

You can also redeclare a local variable without assigning a value to it so you can reassign the variable in both its scope level and descendant scope levels. Redeclaring a local variable without assigning a value to it sets its value to nil.

In the following code, Luau shadows the local variable fruitName in the function getFruitByColor(). The function redeclares fruitName as a new shadow variable and sets its value to nil. The function has a descendant scope level, a for loop, that assigns a value to fruitName. After the for loop, the function returns the fruitName shadow variable. Throughout the entire function, fruitName is the same local variable that doesn't overwrite the initial fruitName local variable.

local fruitName = "Chocolate"
local fruitTable = {
    Lemon = "Yellow",
    Apple = "Red",
    Orange = "Orange"
}

local function getFruitByColor(color)
    local fruitName
    for key, value in fruitTable do
        if value == color then
            fruitName = key
        end
    end
    return fruitName
end

local fruit = getFruitByColor("Yellow")
print(fruit) -- Lemon
print(fruit .. ", not " .. fruitName) -- Lemon, not Chocolate

kid.simple: Scope means where in your script a variable can be seen and used. A `local` variable only exists inside the block of code where you made it, like inside a function or loop. Inner blocks can see variables from outer blocks, but outer blocks cannot peek inside inner ones. Understanding scope stops a lot of confusing bugs, like a variable suddenly being `nil`.
kid.analogy: Scope is like rooms in a house with one-way windows. From a small inner room you can look out and see everything in the bigger rooms around you, but people in the big rooms cannot see into the small room.
keyPoints: A block is the body of a function, loop, or `if` statement.
Local variables can be used in the block where they are made and in any blocks inside it, but not outside.
Global variables (no `local`) can be used anywhere in the same script, but not from other scripts.
Prefer `local`: it is faster (globals can make a busy loop more than 10% slower) and is cleaned up when its block ends.
To share values between scripts, use a ModuleScript.
Capturing: a function can use a local variable from the block around it. That captured variable is called an upvalue.
Shadowing: making a new `local` with the same name inside an inner block. The outer one is not changed.
`const` variables follow the same scope rules as `local` ones.

terms.scope: The area of code where a variable or function can be used.
terms.block: A chunk of code inside a function, loop, or `if`, usually ending with `end`.
terms.parent block / child block: A child block sits inside a parent block. A loop inside a function is the function's child block.
terms.local scope: Only usable in the block where it was made (and blocks inside it).
terms.global scope: Usable anywhere in the same script.
terms.hash lookup: A slower way Luau finds global variables, by searching for the name each time.
terms.capture: When a function uses a local variable from outside itself.
terms.upvalue: A local variable from an outer block that a function uses (captures).
terms.shadowing: Making a new local with the same name in an inner block. Inside, the new one hides the outer one; outside, the outer one is unchanged.
terms.ModuleScript: A special script that returns values or functions other scripts can load with `require`.

example.title: See scope and shadowing in action
example.code:
local score = 10 -- local to the whole script

local function addBonus()
	-- This function can see score from the outer block (capture)
	score += 5
	local bonusText = "Bonus added!" -- only exists inside this function
	print(bonusText)
end

addBonus()
print(score) --> 15
print(bonusText) --> nil (it was local to addBonus)

for i = 1, 2 do
	local score = 100 -- a new shadow variable, only inside the loop
	print("Loop score:", score) --> 100
end

print("Real score:", score) --> 15 (unchanged by the loop)
explain: `score` is made at the top, so everything below can use it.
`addBonus` captures `score` and changes it from 10 to 15.
`bonusText` lives only inside `addBonus`, so printing it outside gives `nil`.
Inside the loop, `local score = 100` makes a separate variable that hides the outer one.
After the loop, the original `score` is still 15.

watchOut: Using a variable outside the block it was made in. It will be `nil`; declare it in an outer block instead.
Accidentally shadowing. Writing `local score = ...` inside a function makes a new variable instead of changing the outer one.
Forgetting `local` inside a function. That makes a global by mistake.
Expecting another script to see your variables. Use a ModuleScript to share them.
